assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned a superconducting artificial atom coupled to a microwave resonator into a controllable quantum-optics platform: strong coupling, dispersive readout, and the architecture now used in leading quantum processors. The idea is original (theory by Blais and collaborators with Schoelkopf's group), cleanly demonstrated, and its impact on quantum technology and on microwave quantum optics is large and lasting. From my own field I judge it a foundational enabling discovery, not a mere engineering advance.
assessment.attribution: Blais supplied the central theoretical proposal, Schoelkopf's group the first strong-coupling and dispersive-readout experiments, and Wallraff the experimental strong-coupling demonstration with the resonator architecture and many follow-ups. A three-person split is plausible. I recall the original experiments being with Wallraff as lead author in Schoelkopf's group, which complicates credit between those two; I have not verified the details independently.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of independent replication across many laboratories and platforms, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue, though the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject and the committee should consider spreading recognition across areas.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may argue for waiting or for a different field.
Allocation of credit between Schoelkopf and Wallraff, and the weight of theory versus experiment, is not fully settled by the supplied credit list.
I have a professional interest in this field (Chalmers, WACQT), so my assessment may carry bias toward it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, followed by the HgTe observation, opened the field of topological band theory and has had a profound conceptual impact on condensed matter physics, with wide influence on materials, spintronics and topological quantum computing ideas.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction and introduced the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realization (with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and Konig et al. in HgTe). The BHZ proposers are not among the credited names here, and Hasan's 3D topological insulator observation is a separate step, so any three-person configuration leaves out important contributors. I propose Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the cleanest theory-plus-experiment core.
assessment.maturity: Well established by many independent experiments and mature theory; recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Hasan and of the HgTe theory proposers makes the allocation contestable.
The relation of the 2D and 3D topological insulator discoveries to the 2016 topological-phases prize needs careful handling.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal of the trapped-ion quantum computer by Cirac and Zoller and its experimental realization, including entangling gates, algorithms and error correction, established a leading platform for quantum computation and simulation. The impact on quantum information science is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller provided the original theoretical scheme; Blatt led much of the experimental realization of gates and algorithms, with other groups (notably Wineland's, already recognised in 2012) also central. Three names are plausible, though Zoller also appears under other candidates, and the overlap with the prior prize is a point to weigh.
assessment.maturity: Mature, widely confirmed and now commercially relevant; recognition is timely though partly overlapping with the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Nobel Prize to Haroche and Wineland may reduce novelty.
Credit between theory, experiment and competing ion-trap groups is not fully resolved here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, programmable Hubbard models, single-site resolved microscopy) created a new way to study strongly correlated many-body physics, with deep links to condensed matter theory.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the Greiner-Bloch observation of the Mott transition are the core; Bloch and Greiner built the experimental platform and microscopy, while Esslinger and Cirac also have strong claims. With five credited names a three-person prize forces difficult choices; I propose Bloch, Zoller and Greiner, but I am not certain this is the fairest set.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with broad independent confirmation, extensive follow-up and a stable interpretation.
uncertainties: Five strong credited names exceed the three-laureate limit and the choice of subset is contestable.
Whether its scientific impact is now primarily methodological rather than a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands, correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity in a tunable system, launching moire materials as a new field with very rapid, broad impact.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulators and superconductivity. Andrei's contributions to the twisted-graphene scanning and early work are significant, so the three-name set omits a serious claimant.
assessment.maturity: Strong early confirmation by many groups, but the pairing mechanism remains debated and the field is still evolving, so some caution about timing is warranted.
uncertainties: Omission of Eva Andrei and of others (e.g. Cory Dean, Pablo Jarillo-Herrero's collaborators) creates a credit dispute.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of quantized conductance in ballistic quantum point contacts was a clean and original demonstration of mesoscopic quantum transport and became a building block for later nanoscale devices, including quantum dots and spin qubits. It sits close to my own background in mesoscopic physics.
assessment.attribution: Two independent groups (van Wees et al. in Delft and Wharam, Pepper et al. in Cambridge) published the effect almost simultaneously in 1988. The credited names support a fair configuration, but Wharam and Pepper are on one paper, and van Wees' group has other co-authors not listed here, so some credit remains unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and long confirmed; arguably delayed recognition, but its fundamental impact has been absorbed into textbook knowledge.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as sufficiently prize-worthy decades later.
Co-author credit beyond the three listed names (not available to me) may matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution links fundamental quantum physics (no-cloning, entanglement) to a practical technology for secure communication, with Bennett-Brassard's BB84 protocol and Ekert's entanglement-based protocol as conceptual cornerstones, and with extensive experimental follow-up.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84; Ekert independently proposed the entanglement-based E91 protocol. Pan's satellite and long-distance experiments are the practical demonstration but a three-person prize centred on the founding ideas looks most defensible. I note possible overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement experiments.
assessment.maturity: Theory is mature, practical deployment is still developing, and the security of real implementations has known loopholes, so the experimental maturity is mixed.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics on entangled photons.
Whether physics (as opposed to computer science or cryptography) is the best home for the prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays have made a highly controllable platform for quantum simulation and computation, with fast recent progress in entangling gates and error-corrected logical qubits.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and colleagues proposed the Rydberg gate and blockade mechanism; Browaeys and Lukin demonstrated blockade and large programmable arrays. Saffman's contributions are also central, so the three-person subset is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing but still young; recognition may be premature relative to optical lattice and trapped-ion work.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the pace of ongoing experimental results.
Allocation among Saffman, Lukin, Browaeys and Zoller is not clear.
